title: A Ticket, and a Missed Train

lessons.title: билет туда и обратно (bilét tudá i obrátno) — a return ticket
lessons.gloss: a return ticket — literally 'a ticket there and back'; a ticket до a place and на a train, bought at the till

segments.text: Say "a ticket", "a train" and "the till". (Bilét. Póyezd. Kássa.) Then ask the way to the till. (Kak proytí k kásse?)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: туда и обратно

segments.text: туда и обратно — tudá i obrátno — "there and back". At the till it is a return ticket:

— Один билет до Москвы, пожалуйста. — Туда и обратно? — odín bilét do Moskvý, pozhálusta. tudá i obrátno? — One ticket to Moscow, please. Return? — Да, туда и обратно. — da, tudá i obrátno — Yes, a return.
A single is в одну сторону — v odnú stóronu — "in one direction".

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: до a place, на a train

segments.text: A ticket goes до the place, as far as it, and the place changes as it did after до in the street: светофор, до светофора; Москва, до Москвы.
A ticket is на the train or the bus, and поезд and автобус keep their plain form: билет на поезд, билет на автобус — bilét na póyezd, bilét na avtóbus.
— Сколько стоит билет? — Тысяча рублей.
Skólko stóit bilét? — "How much is the ticket?" Týsyacha rubléy — "A thousand roubles." After тысяча, рубль takes the counting form рублей.

обратно is the adverb of обратный, "reverse, return". EtymDB 2.1 lists обратный without a parent; by the usual account it is об-, "around", with the root of вертеть, "to turn", from Proto-Indo-European wert-: a ticket that turns round. туда is "to that place", on the same pointing stem as тот.

segments.instruction: Tudá i obrátno. Then a single: V odnú stóronu.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *Tudá i obrátno.* Then a single: *V odnú stóronu.*]

segments.text: "A return ticket"? (Билет туда и обратно.) "A ticket to Moscow"? (Билет до Москвы.) "A ticket for the train"? (Билет на поезд.)

lessons.title: я опоздал на поезд (ya opozdál na póyezd) — I've missed the train
lessons.gloss: I've missed the train — literally 'I was late for the train'; reporting a problem with the perfective past, the result that is still true now

segments.text: Say "to be late" and "to lose". (Opázdyvat. Teryát.) Then "a return ticket for the train". (Bilét na póyezd tudá i obrátno.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: я опоздал на поезд

segments.text: Я опоздал на поезд. — ya opozdál na póyezd — I've missed the train. A woman says Я опоздала на поезд.
Russian says "I was late for the train", with на, as on a ticket. Опоздать is the perfective partner of опаздывать: one lateness, and the train is gone.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a problem is a result

segments.text: English often reports a problem with "I have": I've lost, it has gone. Russian uses the perfective past, because the result is still true now:
К сожалению, я потерял билет. — k sozhaléniyu, ya poteryál bilét — Unfortunately I've lost my ticket. Поезд уже ушёл. — póyezd uzhé ushól — The train has already left.
Потерял is the partner of терять; ушёл, of уходить.
— Извините, у меня проблема. Я опоздал на поезд. — Ничего. Есть поезд через час.

U menyá probléma — "I have a problem", literally "at me, a problem". Nichevó. Yest póyezd chérez chas — "Never mind. There's a train in an hour." Есть, "there is", is the present of быть that Russian does say aloud. When it is serious: Помогите, пожалуйста!
опоздать is о- with the root of поздно, "late". EtymDB 2.1 lists опоздать without a parent; the usual account takes поздно back to a Proto-Slavic pozdŭ and relates it to Latin post, "after".

segments.instruction: Ya opozdál na póyezd, then a woman: Ya opozdála na póyezd.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *Ya opozdál na póyezd*, then a woman: *Ya opozdála na póyezd.*]

segments.instruction: Izvinítye, u menyá probléma. Póyezd uzhé ushól.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *Izvinítye, u menyá probléma. Póyezd uzhé ushól.*]

segments.instruction: a problem of your own at a station, with one perfective verb
segments.source: [YOU SAY: a problem of your own at a station, with one perfective verb]

segments.text: "I've missed the train"? (Я опоздал на поезд.) "I've lost my ticket": which aspect? (Perfective, потерял: it is still lost.) "I have a problem"? (У меня проблема.)

lessons.title: Review — a ticket, and a train that left without you
lessons.gloss: at the station — a return ticket до a place and на a train, then a missed train and a lost ticket reported in the perfective

segments.text: Ask for one return ticket to Moscow. (Odín bilét do Moskvý, tudá i obrátno, pozhálusta.)

Two lessons, and the station can be handled out loud. A ticket goes до a place and на a train; a return is туда и обратно. And when it goes wrong, the perfective past says what happened and is still true: я опоздал на поезд (ya opozdál na póyezd), я потерял билет.
— Извините, я опоздала на поезд. Как пройти к кассе? — Идите прямо, потом налево.
The whole trip so far in two lines: a problem in the perfective, a question about the way, and an answer in two steps.

segments.instruction: Izvinítye, ya opozdála na póyezd. Kak proytí k kásse?
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *Izvinítye, ya opozdála na póyezd. Kak proytí k kásse?*]

segments.instruction: Dva biléta na póyezd, tudá i obrátno.
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *Dva biléta na póyezd, tudá i obrátno.*]

segments.instruction: Pochemú ty opozdál? Explain what happened, then what followed, with poétomu
